title: Compiled vs Interpreted: How C# and Python Run
oneLiner: Roslyn to IL to JIT or AOT for C#, source to bytecode on a virtual machine for Python, and why "compiled language" is the wrong question.
keyTakeaway: Compiled and interpreted describe implementations, not languages, and most real runtimes mix both. C# is compiled by Roslyn to intermediate language (IL), and at run time the .NET JIT compiles each method to native code on first call, first quickly (tier 0) and then again with full optimization once the method proves hot (tier 1). Native AOT does that compilation at build time instead. CPython compiles Python source to bytecode and then interprets the bytecode in a loop, which is why pure Python is typically 10 to 100 times slower than C# on tight loops.
explanation:
A compiler translates a whole program into another form before it runs. An interpreter reads a program and carries it out as it goes. Ahead-of-time (AOT) compilation to machine code (the CPU's own binary instructions), as C, C++, Rust and Go do, gives fast startup and fast steady-state code but produces a binary per operating system and CPU. Pure interpretation is portable and quick to start, but every operation pays for decoding and dispatch. A just-in-time (JIT) compiler sits between: it compiles to machine code while the program runs, so it can target the exact CPU it's on and optimize based on how the code is actually used.

C# takes the managed route. Roslyn, the C# compiler (also what powers IDE analyzers), parses your code, binds names and types, reports errors, and emits an assembly: a .dll containing IL, a stack-based instruction set that isn't tied to any CPU, plus metadata describing every type and method. When the app runs, the CLR (Common Language Runtime, the engine that runs .NET programs) loads the assembly and, the first time each method is called, the RyuJIT compiler (.NET's JIT) turns that method's IL into native x64 or ARM64 code. That's why the first call to anything is slower than the second.

Since .NET Core 3.0 the JIT is tiered. Tier 0 compiles quickly with few optimizations, so startup is fast. The runtime counts calls, and once a method has been called 30 times it is recompiled in the background at tier 1 with full optimization (inlining, which copies small methods into their callers; register allocation, which keeps values in CPU registers; loop optimizations) and calls switch to the new code. Methods with loops that run long can be swapped mid-loop through on-stack replacement (OSR), which swaps optimized code in while the loop is still running. Since .NET 8, dynamic profile-guided optimization (PGO) is on by default: tier 0 code records which types and branches actually occur, and tier 1 uses that, for example to inline the one implementation an interface call nearly always hits.

Two options move work to build time. ReadyToRun ships precompiled native code inside the assembly to cut startup, and the JIT can still recompile hot methods at tier 1. Native AOT (ahead of time) compiles the whole app to a single native executable with no JIT at run time: fast startup and low memory, good for containers and command-line tools, but it trims (removes) unused code, and anything that generates code at run time (Reflection.Emit, some serializers and dependency-injection containers) must be avoided or replaced by source generators.

CPython, the standard Python, also compiles first. It tokenizes and parses the source into an abstract syntax tree (a tree that represents the structure of the code), compiles that to bytecode in code objects, and caches the bytecode of imported modules as .pyc files in __pycache__. Then the interpreter, a big loop in C, executes the bytecode on a stack-based virtual machine, one instruction at a time, with every value a heap object whose type is checked at run time. Python 3.11 added a specializing adaptive interpreter that rewrites hot instructions into type-specific versions (adding two ints, say), and 3.13 added an experimental JIT that is off by default. PyPy is an alternative Python with a tracing JIT.

Linking is the other half of building native code: see Linkers, Libraries and Loading for how separately compiled pieces become one program.
